relations.mechanism: Demand for Nvidia's chips is real today: Google paid roughly double the market rate for Nvidia capacity while cheaper TPUs were available, a costly revealed preference rather than paper demand. What makes the revenue less secure than the order book implies is how it is financed. Private credit funded the compute platform, a $38 billion Apollo transaction in late May and a $35 billion first tranche from Apollo and Blackstone, so part of the marginal buyer's spending rests on lenders rather than on end customers. Between the ordered chips and working compute sits a power bottleneck, and depreciation schedules may lag obsolescence. The Call therefore prices the revenue as financed, not recurring: once the bottleneck clears, the question is whether end customers keep absorbing capacity at market-rate financing.
alternatives: The demand is structural, not financed: a visibility window that extends a full year across the customer base is harder to manufacture than one customer's beat (the case Invest in Assets makes).

Most of the marginal demand is not end-customer demand at all: future revenue is financed through a circular off-balance-sheet arrangement, so the orders overstate what customers will pay (the case Michael Burry makes).
The shortage is real and the financing is beside the point: Nvidia ramps production continuously and still cannot follow demand, so recurrence holds as long as supply lags (the case Kris makes).
